scenario: Today's generative track turns on two questions: whether generated identifiers and reasoning actually improve ranking, and whether a large model acting as a shopping guide can be pulled off course by surface cues. One paper adds only a multiple-choice task to the learning objective so SID generation also learns relative comparison; another aligns the tokenizer to retrieval first, then deploys it in industrial video search. Reasoning optimization starts rewarding each sentence for how it changes the likelihood of the target identifier, while a reinforcement-learning study shows that ratio-based objectives can collapse training and that the update itself needs to be bounded. An audit finds that shopping recommenders still favor longer product descriptions after relevance is controlled, and that product advice cannot be judged only by whether a reply names the community-listed item, because naming it is not the same as selecting it.

papers.title: Keep it Simple! A Multiple-Choice Task can Benefit Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Wei-Hsiang Huang, Jyun-Yu Jiang, Pu-Jen Cheng
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation has recently witnessed growing interest in generative retrieval. One of the most popular approaches is to autoregressively generate the semantic identifiers (SIDs) of items as recommendations. Existing efforts mainly rely on semantic alignment, sophisticated architectural designs, and extensive hyperparameter tuning. However, the conventional learning framework for generative models could have foundational limitations. Specifically, most generative models directly predict target items without explicitly learning negative compositions and relative ranking signals. This is not well aligned with the philosophy of Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR), which emphasizes the importance of relative rankings between positive and negative samples. In this paper, we show that adding a simple multiple-choice auxiliary task into the learning objective can effectively address this issue. With minimal adaptation, we introduce Task Identifiers and Candidate Constructions to synthesize training data for the multiple-choice auxiliary task. In addition, we provide theoretical analysis of the fundamental benefits of the multiple-choice auxiliary task from the perspectives of information theory and compositional generalization. Extensive experiments on four publicly available benchmark datasets show that our approach can improve TIGER, a conventional generative recommendation model, by 4.9% to 79% in NDCG@10.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders often predict the target item's SID directly and never explicitly learn negatives or relative ranking, which sits poorly with the idea behind BPR, where the rank of a positive against negatives matters. Adding a simple multiple-choice auxiliary task to the learning objective, and synthesizing its training data with task identifiers and candidate construction, supplies that comparison signal with only a small change. A theoretical analysis from information theory and compositional generalization also argues that the auxiliary task helps the model learn a more stable and composable representation. On four public datasets, NDCG@10 rises 4.9% to 79% relative to the conventional generative model TIGER, lowest on MovieLens and highest on Yelp. Gains first rise with more candidates, then saturate. The results are already competitive with mainstream generative recommenders, and they do not rely on heavy tuning. For generative recommenders, adding relative comparison can come before a more elaborate architecture.

papers.title: CARE: Contrastive-Anchored Residual Encoding with Listwise Reconstruction for Retrieval-Oriented Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Yuan Xu, Dawei Chen, Xiaoguang Lin, Xin Chen, Yulong Ou, Haijun Wu
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval replaces nearest-neighbor search with the generation of a document's semantic ID (SID), so the SID tokenizer bounds what the retriever can recall. Common SID constructions (residual k-means, RQ-VAE, finite scalar quantization, capacity balancing) optimize criteria defined on document embeddings alone and do not control whether a query can still find its relevant documents after quantization. We propose two retrieval-oriented SID tokenizers. CARE-SID (Contrastive-Anchored Residual Encoding for Semantic IDs) quantizes in a retrieval-aligned space: a zero-initialized residual alignment network is trained with a query-document contrastive loss before quantization, an anchor loss and a reconstruction target fixed to the original embedding prevent drift and collapse, and reference-vector rating residual quantization assigns the codes. CARE-LR (CARE with Listwise Reconstruction) then distills, for each training query, the similarity distribution that the original embeddings induce over a candidate list into the SID reconstructions, through a function-preserving layer-resolved head. Both keep a document-only encoding interface. We judge SIDs without training a generator, by row-budget recall in a bucketing view (the partition) and a reconstruction view (the SID with its reconstruction). In offline evaluation on industrial video search data, both tokenizers achieve higher reconstruction-view recall than residual k-means, and CARE-LR improves further on CARE-SID, mainly through the listwise distillation. A comparison of two document embeddings shows that contrastive alignment helps most when the embedding has not been trained on search data, and that the embedding affects SID recall far more than the quantizer. CARE-SID is deployed in the generative retrieval stage of an industrial video search system.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval produces a document's SID, so where the tokenizer puts quantization error directly limits what can still be recalled. Common SID methods quantize residual codes on document embeddings alone and do not check whether a query can still find its relevant documents after quantization. CARE-SID first trains contrastive alignment in a retrieval-aligned space, then quantizes, while encoding still uses only the document's own embedding. In offline evaluation, reconstruction-view Recall@10 is 2.48 points higher than RQ-KMeans, and the tokenizer is used in the generative retrieval stage of an industrial video search system, where new videos can be encoded incrementally with the same weights. Listwise distillation can raise the score further, but the present gain mainly follows the reconstruction path; end-to-end benefit for a generator that consumes only integer SIDs still needs confirmation. The choice of embedding moves SID recall far more than the choice of quantizer, and contrastive alignment helps most when the embedding was not trained on search data.

papers.title: Label-Free Detection of Structural Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Randomized Paraphrasing: The Case of Verbosity
papers.authors: Carlos Peláez-González, David Herrera-Poyatos, Francisco Herrera, Andrés Herrera-Poyatos
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as recommenders in e-commerce and conversational shopping systems, where they select a product from a set of retrieved candidates described in natural language. Their decisions should depend on relevance to the user query, but may also be influenced by surface-level properties of the descriptions, such as their length. Detecting such structural biases is difficult because relevance labels are rarely available. We propose a label-free framework to audit LLM-based recommender systems for structural bias. Candidate descriptions are rewritten by randomly assigned paraphrasing models and presented in random order. We prove that, if the recommender's choice is invariant to these rewritings, every paraphraser is selected with equal probability, yielding a statistical test that requires no relevance labels. A four-step statistical pipeline tests this property and quantifies the contribution of each description feature while controlling for query-product relevance. We apply the framework to verbosity bias on 20{,}000 product queries and nine recommender LLMs from five model families. After controlling for the measured relevance signals, description length has a positive effect on selection in all nine models, increasing the odds of selection by up to 38% per standard deviation of length. Relevance remains the primary driver of recommendations, while verbosity acts as a consistent secondary signal whose strength depends on the model family. Since the framework needs only black-box access and no annotations, it can be run as a routine audit of deployed shopping assistants, and we provide an auditing protocol with cost and sample-size guidance.
papers.summary: When a large model picks a product from retrieved e-commerce candidates, the choice should depend on relevance to the user query, but the length of a description can also quietly add weight. Relevance labels are rarely available, so this kind of structural bias is hard to measure directly. This work rewrites each product description with randomly assigned paraphrasers and presents the candidates in random order. If the recommender is truly invariant to rewriting, every paraphraser should be chosen with equal probability, and no relevance labels are required. On 20,000 product queries and nine recommender models from five families, description length still has a positive effect in all nine models after controlling for the measured relevance signals. Each extra standard deviation of length raises the odds of selection by as much as 38%, and by about 12% in the least sensitive model. Relevance remains the main driver, and verbosity is a secondary signal that varies by model family, so the test can be run as a routine audit of a shopping assistant.

papers.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhuoyang Li, Teng Shi, Jiakai Tang, Weijie Yu, Guofu Xie, Xiao Zhang, Lei Kou, Yang Yu, Lei Shen, Xin Chen, Bing Wang, Xiaoyi Zeng, Jun Xu
papers.abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.
papers.summary: When generative recommenders add reasoning, existing methods usually reward a whole trajectory from the final recommendation, so they never measure how much each sentence helps the target SID, and different trajectories in a group often get nearly the same reward. This work measures predictive gain: how much each reasoning sentence changes the log-likelihood of the target SID. It then optimizes reasoning with that signal, and a custom causal attention computes the reward without decoding the recommendation again. An auxiliary task further strengthens prediction on trajectories whose cumulative gain is near zero. Average relative gains over the strongest baseline on each of three public benchmarks range from 2.7% to 6.2%. On the Movies data, where competing methods often drop after reasoning is turned on, the gains stay positive. For teams adding reasoning to generative recommendation, the reward should be the sentence's actual contribution to the prediction, not only whether the final item was ranked correctly.

papers.title: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models
papers.authors: Pengfei Zheng, Wuchao Li, Shiyao Wang, Honghui Bao, Hongyi Xie, Jiaxin Deng, Xingmei Wang, Jinghao Zhang, Yufei Ye, Ruiming Tang, Guorui Zhou, Han Li, Kun Gai, Defu Lian
papers.abstract: Traditional cascaded recommender systems balance accuracy and efficiency over large item spaces, but misaligned stage-wise objectives hinder end-to-end optimization. Generative recommendation unifies these stages in an autoregressive framework, providing a natural interface for reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the entire generation process. However, directly applying RL often leads to unstable optimization and degraded recommendation quality. We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and other ratio-based objectives through a unified logit-gradient view. We identify three issues: (i) clipped surrogates create dead-gradient regions, under-utilizing samples; (ii) negative-advantage updates can become effectively unbounded as importance ratios grow, allowing a small subset of negatives to dominate optimization; and (iii) ratio-based control lacks sensitivity to absolute policy confidence, so updates on high-confidence cases may fail to vanish. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose \emph{Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization} (GBPO), a simple objective with stop-gradient normalization that is simultaneously (a) fully gradient-active, (b) sign-symmetrically bounded for both positive and negative updates, and (c) explicitly confidence-weighted under current policy probabilities. This ensures that updates gracefully vanish for $\pi\!\to\!1$ positives and $\pi\!\to\!0$ negatives. Across the evaluated settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation performance with more stable training than competing RL methods.
papers.summary: Applying reinforcement learning directly to generative recommendation often makes ratio-based objectives unstable: clipping can zero the gradient on some samples, and negative-advantage updates can grow with the importance ratio, so a few negatives dominate training. GBPO uses stop-gradient, confidence-aware normalization so that both positive and negative updates stay bounded, and the update shrinks when the policy is already confident. On three Amazon datasets, HR@10 rises 0.71 to 2.21 percentage points over supervised TIGER. On Steam, it was the only method that avoided both performance collapse and a non-finite loss in every repeated run. With a continuous reward or a different teacher model, all fifteen competing runs tripped the collapse rule. For reinforcement post-training of an SID generator, stabilizing the update geometry matters more than clipping the ratio more aggressively.

papers.title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
papers.authors: Assaf Hallak, Yftah Ziser, Gal Chechik
papers.abstract: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.
papers.summary: Matching a product name in a reply to a community-listed item cannot tell whether the advice is good: several products may fit, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When a community-listed alternative is shown beside a model's own sampled car recommendation, with sources and order hidden, six models prefer that alternative in 1.9% to 6.5% of eligible disagreements, consistently in both presentation orders. This work splits advice into the user's stated needs, assumptions the model added, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, and lists 19 failure modes with the evidence needed to assess them. It looks only at the request and the written reply, without access to the model's internals. Naming a reference product is not the same as selecting it, and how the answer is extracted or the candidate list is built also changes the score. To improve product advice, first separate a missing candidate from a candidate that was generated and then chosen wrongly.
